findings.situation: A filer whose only nonrecourse loan is qualified nonrecourse financing borrowed to hold real property would answer no, so box 32b gets checked even though the instructions treat that financing as an exception.
findings.source_text: Question: 'Answer no if any of these is invested in it: a nonrecourse loan used to finance the business, buy property used in it, or buy the business, that is not secured by your own property ... and that you are not personally responsible to repay'. i1040sc pp. 14-15: 'However, there is an exception for certain nonrecourse financing borrowed by you in connection with holding real property. See the Instructions for Form 6198 and Pub. 925.'
findings.why: The question leaves out the exception for qualified nonrecourse financing on real property. Because of that, a truthful answer would mark amounts as not at risk when the at-risk rules count them as at risk, and the 32b line would be set when it should not be.

findings.situation: A filer whose only business credit is tied to employees (for example a work opportunity credit) is told by the label to leave out 'the employment credits asked about with the special items of this Schedule C', but told by the help to 'Count any of them: a credit tied to employees'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 116, Line 6a: "The general business credit consists of a number of credits that usually apply only to individuals who are partners, shareholders in an S corporation, self-employed, or who have rental property. See Form 3800 or Pub. 334."
findings.why: The text treats the general business credit as one group of credits on Form 3800 and carves out no employment credits, so the label and the help point to opposite answers for this filer. Reading the label gives no and reading the help gives yes, and only the yes triggers the Form 3800 refusal on sc.line1.

findings.situation: A retired public safety officer had 2025 premiums for this business's plan paid from retirement plan distributions that were nontaxable (up to $3,000), and reports them in the total because the question never excludes them.
findings.source_text: f7206 (2025) line 1: "But don't include the following... • Any amounts paid, not to exceed $3,000, from retirement plan distributions that were nontaxable because you are a retired public safety officer."; i1040gi p. 95: "Amounts paid for health insurance coverage from retirement plan distributions that were nontaxable because you are a retired public safety officer can't be used to figure the deduction."
findings.why: The question lists the subsidized-plan months and long-term care as exclusions but omits this one. A truthful answer therefore overstates line 1 and line 3 by up to $3,000.

findings.situation: In December 2025 a filer prepaid premiums for 2026 coverage and includes them, because the question asks for the total 'paid in 2025' without limiting it to coverage for 2025.
findings.source_text: f7206 (2025) line 1: "Enter the total amount paid in 2025 for health insurance coverage established under your business ... for 2025 for you, your spouse, and your dependents."
findings.why: The form counts only 2025 payments for 2025 coverage. The question's wording also takes in 2025 payments for coverage of other years.

findings.situation: A business claims the Form 4136 credit for a nontaxable use that is not off-road use, such as taxable fuel it exported, and so truthfully answers no to a question about fuel used off the road in equipment or a boat.

Attach Form 4136."; i4136 p. 2: "Exported taxable fuel. The claim rates for exported taxable fuel are listed on lines 1d, 2c, 3e, 4d, 14b, 16a, and 16b."
findings.why: The tax text gives off-highway business use only as one example of a nontaxable purpose, but the question makes off-road use the whole test. findings.situation: On a joint return where this business and its health plan belong to the spouse, a filer cannot tell whether 'you' in 'you file Form 2555', 'you were a more-than-2% shareholder of an S corporation', 'you used an optional method' and 'you are a retired public safety officer' means the business owner or the person answering, because only the last item adds '(yours or your spouse's)'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 95: 'Use Form 7206 instead of the Self-Employed Health Insurance Deduction Worksheet ... if any of the following applies ... • You file Form 2555.'; i7206 p. 1: 'You received wages in 2025 from an S corporation in which you were a more-than-2% shareholder.'
findings.why: The conditions apply to the person whose business carries the insurance plan. A filer who reads 'you' as themselves rather than the spouse who owns the business could answer no when the spouse files Form 2555 or is the S corporation shareholder, or yes when only the non-owner meets a condition. The two readings give different gate results.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor who paid only dental, vision or qualified long-term care premiums answers No, because the question asks only about "health insurance" and never says these count.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 94, Line 17: "the amount you paid for health insurance (which includes medical, dental, and vision insurance and qualified long-term care insurance)"
findings.why: An ordinary filer would read "health insurance" as medical coverage only. A No gives zero on line 14, even though Form 7206 lines 1–2 would count those premiums.

findings.situation: A self-employed filer who voluntarily pays Medicare premiums for coverage in their own name answers No, because they don't see Medicare as insurance "established under this business."
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 95: "Medicare premiums you voluntarily pay to obtain insurance in your name that is similar to qualifying private health insurance can be used to figure the deduction."
findings.why: The question doesn't say that Medicare premiums can count as a policy in your own name under the business. A filer would likely answer No, and line 14 would be zero when a deduction is allowed.

findings.situation: The filer runs two or more of their own businesses from the same home, each on its own Schedule C. The question asks only about sharing the area with someone else's business, so the filer truthfully answers no, and the tool could allow up to 300 square feet for each business.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 10: "If you conduct more than one business that qualifies for this deduction in your home, your election to use the simplified method applies to all your qualified business uses of your home. You are limited to a maximum of 300 square feet for all of the businesses you conduct in your home ... Allocate the actual square footage used (up to the maximum 300 square feet) among your qualified business uses"
findings.why: The 300-square-foot cap is shared across all of the filer's own home businesses, and the area must be allocated among them. None of the listed conditions covers the filer's other businesses, so this case is not screened even though the per-business figure needs that allocation.

findings.situation: Spouses run the business as a qualified joint venture and must split the home-office square footage between them. None of the listed items applies, so the filer answers no.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 11, Line 2: "If you and your spouse conducted the business as a qualified joint venture, split the square feet between you and your spouse in the same manner you split your other tax attributes."
findings.why: Line 2 needs a split square-footage figure for qualified joint venture spouses. The question does not ask about that split, and an ordinary filer would not treat a spouse's share as "someone else's business."

locators: p. 10, Line 30; pp. 10-13, Instructions for the Simplified Method Worksheet, Daycare Facility Worksheet, Business use of more than one home, Shared use and Part-year use or area changes; p. 10, Electing to use the simplified method, "on a timely filed, original federal income tax return for that year"
pp. 10-13, Line 30 and the Simplified Method Worksheet

findings.situation: A family daycare provider uses an area regularly for daycare but not exclusively, for example as a family room in the evenings, and so leaves that area out because the question asks only for space used 'regularly and exclusively' or for storage.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 10: 'multiplying the area (measured in square feet) used regularly and exclusively for business, regularly for daycare, or regularly for storage of inventory or product samples, by $5'
findings.why: Daycare space only has to be used regularly; the hours fraction on line 3b handles non-exclusive use. The question names only the exclusive-use and storage cases, so a truthful daycare filer reports too little or zero.

findings.situation: A filer shares the business area with a roommate or spouse who runs a separate qualifying business, or runs this business with a spouse as a qualified joint venture, and enters the whole area used.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 13: 'you may not include the same square feet to figure your deduction as the other person. You must allocate the shared space'; p. 11 Line 2: 'split the square feet between you and your spouse in the same manner you split your other tax attributes'
findings.why: The question asks for 'the square feet of your home used ... for this business' and does not ask for the filer's allocated share. The shared or joint-venture space is then claimed in full by more than one person.

findings.situation: A filer runs two qualifying businesses in the home, each in its own area, for example 200 and 250 square feet, and answers this question truthfully on each Schedule C.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 10: 'You are limited to a maximum of 300 square feet for all of the businesses you conduct in your home that qualify for this deduction. Allocate the actual square footage used (up to the maximum 300 square feet) among your qualified business uses'
findings.why: Each Schedule C gets its own answer, and only the per-answer 300 check applies. Together the two schedules claim 450 square feet against a 300 square-foot limit shared by all the businesses.

findings.situation: A filer used two homes for the same business in 2025 and counts the business area in both homes.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 13: 'If you used more than one home for the same business during 2025, you may elect to use the simplified method for only one home; you must file a Form 8829 ... for any additional home'
findings.why: 'The square feet of your home' does not limit the answer to the single home chosen for the simplified method. Area claimed on Form 8829 for the other home is counted again here.

findings.situation: A filer starts business use partway through the year, moves, or changes the area during the year, as in the Finley example (400 square feet from July 20).
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 13: 'your deduction is limited to the average monthly allowable square footage ... adding the amount of allowable square feet you used in each month and dividing the sum by 12 ... can't take more than 300 square feet into account for any 1 month ... less than 15 days in a month, use -0-'; p. 11 Line 2: 'Do not enter more than 300 square feet or, if applicable, the average monthly allowable square footage'
findings.why: Line 2 needs the average monthly allowable square footage: each month capped at 300, months with under 15 days of use set to zero, and the total divided by 12 (125 in the Finley example). The question asks for the actual area used, which gives 400 in that example.

findings.situation: A filer whose business area was not used for all of 2025 reads 'throughout 2025' and must decide what to report.
findings.source_text: Question: 'used regularly and exclusively for this business ... throughout 2025'
findings.why: The filer can reasonably read this as asking for space used for the whole year, giving 0 for part-year space, or for the space used at any time during the year, giving the full area. Neither reading produces the average monthly allowable square footage that line 2 needs.

findings.situation: A family daycare provider uses part of the home regularly for daycare but not exclusively, so the deduction is allowed, yet the question's parenthetical lists only exclusive business use or inventory/sample storage, and the filer answers no.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 10, Simplified method: "the area (measured in square feet) used regularly and exclusively for business, regularly for daycare, or regularly for storage of inventory or product samples"; p. 11, Line 3b: "If you did not use the part of your home exclusively for providing daycare, complete the Daycare Facility Worksheet"
findings.why: The text treats regular daycare use as a qualifying use even without exclusive use. A filer reading the parenthetical as the definition would answer no, and line 30 would be zero when a deduction is allowed.

findings.situation: A filer uses a room regularly and exclusively for the business but fails another qualification test (for example, it is not the principal place of business), answers yes to the parenthetical, and gets a line 30 deduction.

findings.why: The parenthetical reads as a full test, so a filer who meets only the regular-and-exclusive test answers yes even though the other Pub. 587 tests are not met. The lines then compute a deduction the text does not allow.

findings.situation: A statutory employee (Form W-2 with the box 13 'Statutory employee' box checked) reports that income on this Schedule C, but the question only asks for gross receipts or sales and amounts on Forms 1099.
findings.source_text: i1040sc (2025) p. 5, Line 1, Statutory employees: "Enter your statutory employee income from box 1 of Form W-2 on line 1 of Schedule C and check the box on that line."
findings.why: The wording names Forms 1099-NEC and 1099-K but never W-2 box 1 statutory employee wages, so an ordinary filer would not think of W-2 wages as 'gross receipts or sales' and could answer zero or leave them out. Line 1, and so line 3, would then be understated.

findings.situation: Spouses who elected qualified joint venture treatment each file a separate Schedule C, but the question asks for the gross receipts 'of this business', which a filer would answer with the whole business's receipts.
findings.source_text: i1040sc (2025) p. 3, Making the election: "divide all items of income, gain, loss, deduction, and credit attributable to the business between you and your spouse based on your respective interests in the business... Enter your share of the applicable income, deduction, or (loss) on the appropriate lines of your separate Schedule C"
findings.why: The question says "Gross receipts or sales of this business for 2025" with no limit to the filer's own share, so a qualified joint venture spouse would enter 100% of the receipts. Line 1 on each spouse's schedule must carry only that spouse's share, so the receipts would be overstated or counted twice.

findings.situation: An accrual-method filer incurred commissions in 2025 that it will not pay until 2026, so line 10 needs them but a truthful answer to 'you paid' leaves them out.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 10: "Enter the total commissions and fees for the tax year." (Schedule C item F allows the Accrual method)
findings.why: The text asks for the commissions and fees deductible for the tax year under the filer's accounting method. The question asks only what the filer paid, which matches the cash method only.

findings.situation: A filer who is not a dealer paid a broker's commission to sell a business asset and never capitalized it, so truthfully reports it as 'not capitalized'.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 10: "Generally, commissions and other fees paid to facilitate the sale of property must be capitalized. However, if you are a dealer in property, enter on line 10 ..."
findings.why: 'Not capitalized' reads as a description of what the filer actually did, not as a rule that requires capitalization. Sale-facilitating commissions that must be capitalized therefore get into line 10, and the dealer exception is never explained.

findings.situation: A filer includes commissions paid in 2024 or 2026 (for example, a January 2026 payment), because the question gives no time frame.
findings.source_text: Question: "Commissions and fees you paid (not capitalized and not deducted elsewhere)"; i1040sc p. 7: "Enter the total commissions and fees for the tax year."
findings.why: The question does not limit the amount to the 2025 tax year, so amounts from other years can be included.

findings.situation: An accrual-method business incurs contract labor costs in 2025 that it has not paid by year end, or pays in 2025 for services accrued and deducted in 2024.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 11: "Enter the total cost of contract labor for the tax year." (f1040sc p. 1, line F, Accounting method: Cash / Accrual)
findings.why: The question asks for "Payments" and gives no year, so an accrual filer would report cash paid instead of the cost incurred for the tax year. Unpaid 2025 costs are left out, and payments for prior-year costs may be pulled in.

findings.situation: A filer pays an independent contractor for work that is deducted somewhere other than lines 17, 21, 26 or 37, such as repairs to a home office claimed through Form 8829 on line 30, or labor capitalized into an asset's basis.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 11: "Do not include contract labor deducted elsewhere on your return, such as contract labor includible on line 17, 21, 26, or 37." Question: "(not included on lines 17, 21, 26 or 37)"
findings.why: The instructions give those four lines only as examples ("such as"), but the question makes them a closed list. A truthful filer would include contract labor deducted or capitalized elsewhere, so it would be counted twice.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor makes contributions on their own behalf to a dependent care assistance program and has a deductible amount figured on Form 2441, but answers zero because the question says "not for yourself."
findings.source_text: i1040sc (2025) p. 7, Line 14: "If you made contributions on your behalf as a self-employed person to a dependent care assistance program, complete Form 2441, Parts I and III, to figure your deductible contributions to that program."
findings.why: The instructions put the deductible self-employed dependent care assistance contributions on line 14. The blanket "not for yourself" wording therefore leaves out an amount the line needs.

findings.situation: An employer that claims the small employer health insurance premiums credit on Form 8941 reports its full contributions to employee health plans, so line 14 is not reduced by the credit.

findings.why: The question asks for gross "Contributions to employee benefit programs". Line 14 needs that amount after it is reduced by the Form 8941 credit, so line 28 and the section 179 business income figure come out too high.

findings.situation: A filer who sells at a discounted or sale price and records only the discounted price in gross receipts counts those upfront discounts as 'price reductions you gave customers' on line 2, so the discount is subtracted from line 1 a second time.
findings.source_text: Question: "Returns and allowances (refunds and price reductions you gave customers)"; i1040sc p. 6, Line 2: "A sales allowance is a reduction in the selling price of products, instead of a cash or credit refund."
findings.why: The text treats an allowance as a substitute for a refund, a reduction given after the sale on goods already sold. The question's plain 'price reductions' also covers point-of-sale discounts that are already left out of gross receipts, so the line 3 subtraction double-counts them.

findings.situation: A filer who refunded money that never entered line 1 enters it on line 2, such as a returned deposit, an overpayment, or sales tax handed back, or a refund already netted out of a processor's gross total that the filer used for line 1.
findings.source_text: Question: "refunds ... you gave customers"; i1040sc p. 6, Line 2: "A sales return is a cash or credit refund you gave to customers who returned defective, damaged, or unwanted products."
findings.why: The text limits returns to refunds for products customers returned, which reverse sales counted in gross receipts. The question's open-ended 'refunds you gave customers' takes in refunds that do not reverse a line 1 amount, which understates line 3.

findings.situation: An employer who claims the Work Opportunity Credit, Empowerment Zone Employment Credit, Form 8932 credit or Form 8994 paid leave credit enters gross wages paid, but line 26 needs wages reduced by those credits.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 10, Line 26: "Enter the total salaries and wages for the tax year reduced by the amount of the following credit(s), if applicable. • Work Opportunity Credit (Form 5884). • Empowerment Zone Employment Credit (Form 8844). • Credit for Employer Differential Wage Payments (Form 8932). • Employer Credit for Paid Family and Medical Leave (Form 8994)."

A truthful answer is the figure before the credit reduction, so lines 28 and the section 179 business income limit are understated by the credit amount. The question also does not say that credits passed through from a pass-through entity are not subtracted.

findings.why: The text measures wages for the tax year under the filer's accounting method. Asking for amounts paid in calendar 2025 leaves out wages accrued but unpaid at year end, and it brings in prior-year accruals paid in 2025.

findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer changed method 'for 2025'. A section 481(a) adjustment carried into 2025 from an earlier change still has to be screened out, but this wording does not catch it.

findings.situation: A business that has existed for only one or two prior years, or that has a predecessor entity, averages its gross receipts over a full 3 years or leaves out the predecessor's receipts, gets a figure of $31 million or less, and answers no.

findings.source_text: i1040sc 2025 p. 5, Part I: "If you were a debtor in a chapter 11 bankruptcy case during 2025, see Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Cases in the Instructions for Form 1040"
findings.why: The special rule applies only when the filer was the debtor and only during 2025. The question's 'a chapter 11 bankruptcy case' leaves out both limits, so a creditor or someone with a past case can truthfully answer yes and be screened out without need.

findings.situation: Spouses jointly own and run an unincorporated business and share profits, but have no partnership agreement, made no qualified joint venture election, and do not think of the business as community property.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 2: "Generally, if you and your spouse jointly own and operate an unincorporated business and share in the profits and losses, you are partners in a partnership, whether or not you have a formal partnership agreement."
findings.why: The parenthetical names three formal arrangements. A filer with no agreement or election may decide that none of them applies and answer no, so the gate does not screen out a business that is a partnership by default and belongs on Form 1065.

findings.situation: A filer's Schedule C business includes notary public fees along with other self-employment receipts, such as loan-signing agent fees reported together on the same schedule.
findings.source_text: i1040sc p. 14, Line 31: "Notary public. Do not enter your net profit from line 31 on Schedule SE (Form 1040), line 2, unless you are required to file Schedule SE (Form 1040) because you have other self-employment income."
findings.why: The question asks whether "this business income" is notary fees. A filer whose income is only partly notary fees could fairly answer no, because not all of it is, or yes, because some of it is. The notary self-employment treatment the gate screens for applies whenever notary fees are part of line 31. Statutory employee income cannot be mixed in this way ("You cannot combine these amounts on a single Schedule C", p. 5), but the instructions give no such separation rule for notary fees.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor's Schedule C business has no tips but receives qualified overtime on Form 1099-NEC, so the filer answers yes and the business is counted toward the line 5 count of businesses with tips.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 104, line 5: "Include the qualified tips you and/or your spouse received in the course of a trade or business... If you and/or your spouse received qualified tips in the course of more than one trade or business, complete the Multiple Trades or Businesses Worksheet"; p. 108, line 14b: "Enter on Line 14b only the qualified overtime compensation amount that is included in Form 1099-NEC, box 1, or Form 1099-MISC, box 3"
findings.why: The line cites only line 5, and line 5's per-business count and net income limit apply to qualified tips received in a trade or business. Overtime goes on line 14b, which uses a per-payor worksheet rather than a per-business one. Folding overtime into the question counts businesses that line 5 does not reach.

findings.situation: A business received qualified tips but has a net loss after allocable deductions, so no tip deduction survives for it.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 104: "but only to the extent the trade or business in which you received the qualified tips has net income... Do not reduce it below zero."
findings.why: The phrase "that you would deduct on Schedule 1-A" can be read as "received qualified tips here," which gives yes. It can also be read as "will end up deducting an amount after the net income limit," which gives no. The two readings change whether the business is counted.
